results.title: Nebius Raises On-Demand GPU Prices Up to 21% From October 1: What an H100 Hour Now Costs | ServerCalc
results.author: ServerCalc Editorial
highlights:
# Nebius Raises On-Demand GPU Prices Up to 21% From October 1: What an H100 Hour Now Costs

Nebius lifted pay-as-you-go GPU rates up to 21% on October 1 — H100 to $4.50 an hour, B300 to $9.50 — the second rise since spring as AI capacity sells out.

October 12, 2026 ServerCalc Editorial 5 min read

The capacity squeeze that has been pushing up VPS prices all year sits at the other end of the market too, on the GPU servers that AI workloads run on. One of the larger listed GPU clouds, Nebius, has just moved its on-demand prices again — the second time it has done so since the spring — and the new rates are a useful marker for anyone pricing an AI server rather than a plain VPS.

## What changed

From October 1, 2026, Nebius raised its on-demand, pay-as-you-go rates across its four current Nvidia platforms. On its own published price list the per-GPU-hour numbers now read: H100 NVLink at $4.50, up from $3.85 (about 17%); H200 NVLink at $5.40, up from $4.50 (20%); B200 NVLink at $8.50, up from $7.15 (about 19%); and B300 NVLink at $9.50, up from $7.85 (21%). CPU-only servers were caught in the same round — the AMD EPYC Genoa vCPU now lists at $0.015 per CPU-hour, roughly a quarter more than before. Separately, from October 8 the provider moved preemptible capacity for these platforms onto dynamic spot pricing, so the cheap interruptible tier no longer has a fixed rate.

These are list prices for on-demand use. Committed and reserved terms are quoted separately and run well below the hourly rate; the increase lands hardest on buyers who pay by the hour with no commitment.

...

The hourly figures are small, but GPU servers run continuously and in multiples, so they add up fast. A single H100 left running around the clock for a 730-hour month now costs about $3,285 on demand, against roughly $2,810 before October 1 — close to $475 a month more for the same card. Nvidia's NVLink parts are usually taken eight to a node, and an 8×H100 box now runs $36 an hour, or about $26,280 a month flat out, up from near $22,480 — a jump of roughly $3,800 a month per node.

...

Nebius has not tied the increase to the cost of any one component. Its own executives have described a market where demand outruns supply: the company has said it sold capacity as fast as it could bring it online, and that it could sell its entire 2027 capacity on current deal terms. That is the same story driving the memory and storage shortages we have covered from the VPS side — capacity, power and advanced-packaging supply are the bottleneck, and when a provider cannot build fast enough, the on-demand price is the lever it pulls first.

## What's happening right now

If your GPU bills have been creeping up this year, it isn't your imagination. The most visible signal came from Nebius, which put through a blanket price increase across its GPU cloud services effective October 1, 2026, averaging roughly 20% across multiple chip models including the H100 and H200 — its second round of increases since May, according to EQS Newswire reporting on the announcement.

The more telling detail in that same reporting: some Nebius clients have reserved computing capacity as far ahead as 2028, and the company describes demand visibility stretching beyond 24 months. When customers are willing to book compute two years out at rising prices, the sellers hold the pricing power — and they know it.

results.title: AMD Reportedly Raises GDDR6 Prices for Board Partners
results.author: DrUsmanSaleem
highlights:
# AMD Reportedly Raises GDDR6 Prices for Board Partners

 by 

DrUsmanSaleem

 Oct 11th, 2026 06:54 Discuss (28 Comments) 

AMD has reportedly raised the price of the GDDR6 memory it supplies to its board partners, with the change said to be in effect since October 1. The claim comes from a post on the Chinese forum Board Channels, and it doesn't mention a percentage or a dollar figure. AMD sells its GPUs to add-in board (AIB) partners bundled with memory, so a costlier kit usually ends up in the retail price of the finished card. The timing matches the higher suggested Radeon prices in China reported earlier this week, where the RX 9070 went up by the equivalent of $104 and the RX 9060 XT 8 GB by $45, while the RX 9070 XT was left untouched. NVIDIA, however, apparently hasn't sent its partners a similar notice for GDDR7 this time, and the same post suggests the company may not touch memory pricing again this year. That would be a small relief for GeForce buyers, although NVIDIA already raised GDDR6 and GDDR7 kit prices in July, and the RTX 5090 was tracked at 136% above MSRP globally in early September. AMD's partners have been through this a few times in 2026 already. A 10% hike on Radeon GPU kits was reported for July, and in September there was word of another 10% increase across GPUs, chipsets, and possibly CPUs, tied to rising TSMC wafer costs. AMD hasn't confirmed the latest increase, and we don't know how much or how soon store prices outside China will move.

results.title: AI Compute Cost Outlook: Quarterly Briefing · AgentFlare
highlights:
AI compute is entering a bifurcated market: headline GPU scarcity still supports high hyperscaler pricing, while neocloud competition, commitments, and spot capacity are…

AI compute is entering a bifurcated market: headline GPU scarcity still supports high hyperscaler pricing, while neocloud competition, commitments, and spot capacity are sharply lowering effective costs. Through the next several quarters, inference economics should improve faster than training economics, but capital intensity and networking constraints will keep premium accelerators expensive.

### Pricing is high at the hyperscalers, discounted elsewhere

As of early November, H100 on-demand pricing ranged from roughly $6.88 per GPU-hour at AWS to $11.06 at Google Cloud, versus approximately $3.90–$6.16 across major neoclouds. [5] H200 pricing reached $10.60 per hour on Google Cloud, while B200 capacity was generally available through flexible-start or committed products rather than standard on-demand listings. [4] 

The spread is economically material: hyperscaler list prices averaged nearly twice GPU-cloud medians across H100, H200, and B200 instances. [1] This creates a strong incentive for workload migration, capacity brokering, and multicloud arbitrage—particularly for inference jobs with predictable utilization.

### Effective cost is falling through commitments and utilization

Reservation economics are increasingly decisive. One-year commitments reduce median GPU pricing by about 21%, while three-year commitments cut it by approximately 48% versus on-demand rates. [1] Google’s three-year H100 commitment was listed at $4.86 per GPU-hour, compared with an $11.06 on-demand rate; its H200 equivalent was $4.65 versus $10.60. [4] 

Spot pricing can be dramatically lower—up to 91% below on-demand in some Google configurations—but availability and interruption risk make it unsuitable as the sole basis for distributed training capacity. [4] The next quarters should therefore see more hybrid scheduling: committed capacity for critical training, spot for checkpointable jobs, and neocloud overflow for inference.

...

Token-level cost compression will come primarily from higher utilization, quantization, batching, speculative decoding, and model specialization—not simply lower GPU prices. For example, self-hosting a 120B-class model on eight B200s becomes competitive with a $0.60-per-million-output-token API at roughly 33% sustained utilization under Google flexible-start pricing, rising to about 58% under AWS on-demand economics.

...

Training remains more exposed to system-level bottlenecks: HBM, advanced packaging, liquid cooling, high-speed networking, and power availability. Component inflation has already raised hyperscaler capital budgets; Microsoft estimated roughly $25 billion of incremental 2026 capex from higher component pricing. [9] 

### Outlook: lower effective prices, firm premium hardware

Expect advertised hyperscaler GPU rates to remain sticky through the next two quarters, with selective increases where supply is tight—AWS raised several U.S. GPU configurations by about 15% in October after earlier 2026 increases. [9] Effective market pricing should nevertheless decline as neocloud supply expands and long-term discounts deepen.

The key distinction is between GPU-hour price and cost per useful token. The latter should fall faster, favoring inference platforms with superior utilization and software efficiency rather than operators owning the largest nominal fleet.

### What to watch

- B200 availability and HBM/CoWoS pricing: the earliest signal of whether next-generation supply can relieve premium-GPU scarcity.
- Neocloud utilization and financing: aggressive discounts are sustainable only if power, depreciation, and debt-service costs remain covered.
- Inference utilization thresholds: sustained utilization above 30–60% increasingly determines whether self-hosted deployments beat API pricing. [4]

results.title: AMD GDDR6 Price Hike 2026: Nvidia Holds Off on GDDR7
results.author: Priya Anand
highlights:
AMD has told its graphics card board partners that the price of GDDR6 memory went up effective October 1, 2026, according to reports from Wccftech, TechPowerUp and XenoSpectrum. Nvidia, by contrast, has not sent a comparable notice to its own partners covering GDDR7, the memory standard behind its GeForce RTX 50-series cards, as of October 10-11. Neither company has confirmed the move publicly, and the exact size of the AMD increase has not been disclosed. But the asymmetry between the two GPU makers is already rippling through a supply chain that board partners say gives them little choice but to pass costs along.

...

The core of the story traces back to a report attributed to Board Channels, an industry-sourcing outlet, with related coverage citing BenchLife and a source identified as Bobantang. According to that reporting, AMD notified its board partners, the companies that build and sell Radeon-branded graphics cards, that GDDR6 memory prices supplied alongside AMD’s GPUs increased starting October 1, 2026. Wccftech’s writeup of the Board Channels report states plainly that board partners will now have no other option but to pass the costs on to consumers, since the memory is a required input rather than an optional component they can source independently.

What is missing from every version of this story is a number. No outlet reporting on the October 1 adjustment has published a confirmed percentage, a dollar-per-module figure, or an official AMD statement. AMD has not publicly confirmed the price change at all, let alone its magnitude. That matters because it is tempting to treat any GDDR6 price increase headline as a clean, quantified data point, when in this case the only solid facts are the effective date and the direction of the change. Everything about scale remains, in the careful language used by the outlets covering it, reported rather than confirmed.

It is also worth being precise about what kind of price increase this is. AMD is not announcing a retail MSRP hike on Radeon cards. It is adjusting what board partners, the Asus, Sapphire, PowerColor, XFX and similar companies that actually manufacture and sell Radeon GPUs, pay for the GDDR6 memory AMD supplies as part of the GPU-and-memory kit. Those partners then decide, individually, whether and how much of that increase to pass on to retail pricing. That is a meaningfully different mechanism than a company simply raising sticker prices, and it is why the consumer-facing impact of this GDDR6 price increase could take weeks to show up, and could look different from one Radeon board partner to the next.

...

The second half of the story is Nvidia’s apparent restraint. As of the October 10-11 reporting window, Nvidia has not notified its partners of any new price increase on GDDR7, the memory standard used across its current GeForce RTX 50-series lineup. That too is unconfirmed by Nvidia directly, but it is the consistent thread across every outlet tracking the story, including the Russian-language coverage at overclockers.ru and the Turkish outlet DonanimHaber, both of which independently reported that Nvidia has issued no equivalent GDDR7 notice.

...

Industry speculation, again unconfirmed by Nvidia, suggests the company may avoid a further GDDR7 increase for the rest of 2026, though claims that Nvidia will hold GDDR7 pricing through the end of 2026 remain rumors and Nvidia had not officially confirmed that plan by October 26. If that holds, it would create a temporary pricing divergence between the two GPU makers: AMD absorbing a fresh GDDR6 cost increase on top of an already-tight Radeon supply picture, while Nvidia’s GDDR7 costs stay flat, at least for now, on top of a baseline that was already higher.

...

This October 1 adjustment is not happening in isolation; it fits a pattern of DRAM and GDDR cost pressure that has built steadily across 2026. Industry reports earlier in the year described phased price increases being prepared across both AMD’s and Nvidia’s GPU lineups as memory demand tied to AI data centers outpaced supply. Later in the year, separate reports described AMD applying earlier rounds of GDDR-related cost increases to board partners, months before this October 1 notice: in mid-2026, AMD reportedly added $10 per 8GB to memory-kit pricing, and in July 2026 it reportedly increased GDDR6 memory-kit prices about 10%, its second hike in 6 months; in August 2026, TechTimes reported AMD announced Radeon GPU and GDDR6 kit increases of at least 10% starting that month, with additional increases of 10–15% planned for the second half of 2026; and in September 2026, Silicon Analysts reported GDDR6 prices up roughly 30%. None of those earlier figures are confirmed by AMD either, and this article is not treating them as hard numbers, but the pattern they describe, repeated rounds of memory cost pressure moving through AMD’s supply chain across 2026, is consistent with what is now being reported for October, when TechTimes reported that AMD’s October 1 move was its fourth GDDR6-related price adjustment in 10 months, and Perexp Teamworks reported GDDR6 spot prices of about $7.50/GB by November 2026, up from $2.50 in late 2025 (a secondary report, not an official industry price sheet).

What makes the current moment notable is not that a GDDR6 price increase happened, memory costs moving has been a recurring theme all year, but that it is happening while Nvidia’s GDDR7 costs are reportedly staying flat. For most of 2026, reports on GPU memory pricing described both companies facing similar upward pressure. This is the first clear reported divergence between the two, with AMD moving and Nvidia, for now, not. BigGo also reported that AMD planned another GDDR6 supply-price increase in November 2026, one month after October’s adjustment, a plan that remains unconfirmed.

...

All of these are forward-looking assessments based on the reported pattern so far, not confirmed plans from AMD or Nvidia. Both companies could change course, and neither has committed publicly to any future pricing action.

...

No. AMD has not made a public statement confirming a GDDR6 price increase for board partners. The reporting traces to Board Channels, an industry-sourcing outlet, with related coverage from Wccftech, TechPowerUp and XenoSpectrum.

...

Is Nvidia raising GDDR7 prices too? As of October 10-11, 2026, Nvidia has reportedly not notified its board partners of a GDDR7 price increase. This is also unconfirmed directly by Nvidia, but it is the consistent finding across outlets including overclockers.ru and DonanimHaber.

...

Is this AMD’s first memory price increase in 2026? Reports have described earlier rounds of GDDR-related cost pressure moving through AMD’s supply chain earlier in 2026, though those figures are also unconfirmed by AMD. Reports published October 30–November 2 claimed AMD might raise GPU-and-GDDR6 bundle prices again during November 2026, with the amount, affected models and implementation undisclosed and unconfirmed.

results.title: AMD Radeon GDDR6 Memory Prices Are Going Up, With Graphics Card ...
results.author: Taha
highlights:
The graphics card market is once again facing higher costs, and this time the impact comes from the price of GDDR6 memory modules used in Radeon graphics cards.

AMD has introduced a price increase for the GDDR6 chips it supplies to its assembly partners and manufacturers. The change came into effect on October 1 and is expected to affect graphics card prices sooner rather than later.

## AMD Radeon RX 9000 Graphics Card Prices Expected to Rise

Although GDDR6 memory is used across several generations of AMD graphics cards, from the Radeon RX 5000 series to the latest models, the main impact will fall on the newest cards. Since many older series have been discontinued or are being produced in small numbers, the RX 9000 series, based on the RDNA 4 architecture, will be affected the most.

Graphics card manufacturers do not have much room to respond to this situation. With a direct increase in the cost of the component, the likely result is that graphics card prices will rise to cover the higher cost of memory modules.

In addition, reports suggest that memory is not the only factor pushing prices up.

...

Meanwhile, Nvidia is following a different approach, at least for now. Nvidia, which uses GDDR7 memory for its RTX 50 series GPUs, has not informed its partners of any price changes for the rest of the year.

However, it is worth noting that the RTX 50 series already launched with higher costs because of the starting price of GDDR7 technology itself. Another increase could therefore have caused serious problems for the market.
